# A common-slice quantile bound and a cross-direction tail charge

This is an actual planar convex-body lemma. It uses the same sections of
one body in two cap directions, not independent marginal distributions.
It does not require affine section widths or a triangular body.

## 1. Statement in the canonical coordinates

Let A be a planar convex body of area a. Put

    u=|A intersect {x>=-1}|,
    v=|A intersect {y>=-1}|,

and relabel x,y if needed so u<=v. Define the longitudinal coordinate

    t=-x-y,

let its projection interval on A be [l,h], and let W be the maximum
length of an x-coordinate interval in a section t=constant. Assume

    0<v<a/2.

Then

    |A intersect {t<=2-2W}|<=v,                    (1)
    |A intersect {t>=2}|>=a-v-2W^2.                (2)

If the cut t=-1 is proper and H=h+1, then H>0 and

    W<=2a/(h-l)<2a/H,
    |A intersect {t>=2}|>=a-v-8a^2/H^2.            (3)

The strict width inequality uses l<-1; the displayed tail inequality
is stated weakly for convenient use with other estimates.

The coordinates are appropriate to any chosen pair of canonical
triangle normals v_1=(1,0),v_2=(0,1),v_3=(-1,-1): choosing the other
two normal values as x,y has determinant of absolute value one, and
the remaining normal becomes -x-y. Thus all the areas above agree
with the original canonical areas after such a relabeling.

## 2. Affine selectors inside every section

Choose points P_-,P_+ of A attaining t=l,h. Their connecting segment
is contained in A. Its first coordinate is an affine function X(t),
and its second coordinate is the affine function

    Y(t)=-t-X(t).

For every t in [l,h], the selector point (X(t),Y(t)) belongs to the
actual section. Every other point (x,y) of that section therefore
satisfies

    |x-X(t)|<=W,       |y-Y(t)|<=W.                 (4)

Here W is measured in the x coordinate. The second inequality has
the same constant because x+y=-t is fixed on a section.

Let F be the normalized distribution function of t under uniform area
on A, and put p=v/a<1/2. The distribution has no atoms, and it is
strictly increasing on (l,h): sections of a full-dimensional convex
body have positive length at every interior projection level. Hence
there is a unique t_p in (l,h) satisfying F(t_p)=p.

We claim that each of the affine selectors X,Y has value at most
-1+W at t_p. Consider X first. If its slope is nonpositive and
X(t_p)>-1+W, continuity gives an interval beyond t_p on which the
selector still exceeds that value. Monotonicity then makes every
actual section below that interval entirely satisfy x>=-1, by (4).
The x cap would have area strictly greater than pa=v, contradicting
u<=v. If its slope is positive and X(t_p)>=-1+W, every section
above t_p is entirely captured; its area is (1-p)a>pa, again a
contradiction. Thus X(t_p)<=-1+W. The same argument for Y uses its
own cap area v=pa and gives Y(t_p)<=-1+W.

Adding these two inequalities proves

    -t_p=X(t_p)+Y(t_p)<=-2+2W,
    t_p>=2-2W.

Monotonicity of F gives (1). This proof includes zero selector slopes
and equality at the quantile; no genericity assumption is used.

## 3. Width, area, and the explicit tail correction

The map (t,x) -> (x,-t-x) has determinant of absolute value one, so

    a=int_l^h ell(t) dt,

where ell(t) is the x-coordinate section length. Convexity of A makes
ell concave on [l,h], by interpolation of interval sections. If it
attains its maximum W at t_0, the two affine segments from (l,0)
to (t_0,W) to (h,0) lie below ell. Integrating them gives

    a>=W(h-l)/2.

The same conclusion holds when the maximum occurs at an endpoint;
one of those two triangles then has zero area. Compactness and
one-sided continuity of convex-body section lengths ensure a maximum;
alternatively the same estimate follows by taking a supremizing
sequence of levels. This proves the width bound in (3).

The strip 2-2W<=t<=2 has area at most (2W)W. Combining with (1),

    |A intersect {t<=2}|<=v+2W^2.

Level lines have zero area, so subtracting from a proves (2). If the
cut t=-1 is proper, l<-1, hence h-l>h+1=H. Substitution of the width
bound yields the last assertion of (3).

## 4. Coupling with a known original captured mass

Suppose additionally h>2, the original t>=-1 cap has area w, and
put

    e=a-w>0,
    Delta=sqrt(a)-sqrt(e).

The lower-cap square-root function is concave. At levels -1 and h,
and at the intermediate level 2, this gives

    sqrt(|A intersect {t<=2}|)
       >=sqrt(e)+(3/H)Delta.

Combining with the upper bound |A intersect {t<=2}|<=v+8a^2/H^2
from Section3 yields the explicit necessary inequality

    sqrt(v H^2+8a^2)>=H sqrt(e)+3Delta,

or, equivalently,

    (v-e)H^2-6sqrt(e)Delta H+8a^2-9Delta^2>=0.      (5)

Both sides before squaring are nonnegative, so the equivalence is
exact. This is a quantitative common-slice restriction involving the
whole residual mass below the original cut. It may be combined with
the separate shifted-cover tail bound

    |A intersect {t>=2}|>=a-v-u/4

proved in Section9 of
`candidate 921f72bdedb6df67`
under that note's hypothetical bad-source assumptions.

For instance, if v<=e and 8a^2<9Delta^2, every term on the left of
(5) is nonpositive and its constant term is strictly negative. Such
parameters are impossible for an actual A satisfying this lemma,
independently of the height H. No numerical optimization is used.

## Scope

The requirement v<a/2 is explicit. No claim about that complementary
case is made. The section selector comes from two actual endpoint
points of A; no assumption about section centroids, affine widths, or
an affine approximation is needed. The bound uses actual area and
actual cap fractions, and its coordinate determinant is tracked.
This lemma is a restriction on one convex fiber, not a proof of the
mixed-integer conjecture.
